Article Title: Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman recalls Google co-founder Larry Page’s sci-fi vision from 2015 lunch at SpaceX canteen, Elon Musk says ‘he is right’
Article Text:
The ethics board meeting at SpaceX canteen

Google executives: Larry Page, Sergey Brin, and then-Chief Legal Officer David Drummond.

DeepMind co-founders: Mustafa Suleyman, Demis Hassabis, and Shane Legg.

Jointly Selected Independent Board Member: Elon Musk.

Larry Page’s sci-fi vision for interstellar probes

Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman has recounted a futuristic lunch conversation from 2015 with Google co-founder Larry Page . Revealing that the chat took place at a canteen in SpaceX , Suleyman said that Page envisioned exploring distant galaxies using advanced self-propelling probes by the end of the century. Responding to Suleyman’s story, billionaire entrepreneur Elon Musk echoed the sentiment, stating that Page “might be right” in his bold prediction for human civilization.Recalling the 2015 encounter, Suleyman said that the company chose Musk as one of the three independent members while having a conversation sitting in the canteen at SpaceX headquarters during the very first meeting of DeepMind's AI Ethics and Safety Board. When Google acquired DeepMind in 2014, Suleyman and his co-founders, Demis Hassabis and Shane Legg, made it an explicit condition of the sale that Google establish an ethics committee featuring independent oversight representation.The board structure required mutual agreement between both parties:“Yeah, I remember in 2015 being in the canteen at SpaceX. And we had our first meeting of the Ethics and Safety Board. So when we sold DeepMind to Google, we made it a condition of our acquisition that we would have an Ethics and Safety Board with independent representation on the board,” Suleyman said in a podcast The Builders with Walter Isaacson and Kaleidoscope.“One of those independent members, because Google had to agree, which was obviously Larry, Sergey, and David Drummond at the time. And then me, Demis, and Shane had to jointly agree who those three independents would be. And so we jointly picked Elon as one of them,” he added.Suleyman noted that he remains unsure whether holding those early AI safety discussions at SpaceX headquarters played any role in influencing Musk's subsequent founding of OpenAI.“No idea if that had an influence on the founding of OpenAI or not. But so then we had our morning session and we were sitting down for lunch and I was sitting next to Larry. You know, obviously he was suspicious of me as well because he was like, you know, you’re one of those speciesists,” he recalled.During lunch following the board's morning session, Suleyman found himself sitting next to Larry Page. It was during this meal that Page shared his long-term vision for deep-space exploration driven by advanced technology.“And he said, you know, I think that what you don’t understand, Mustafa, is that by the end of the century, I’m going to be exploring the galaxies at the head of a von Neumann probe,” Suleyman recalled.As Suleyman explained, a von Neumann probe is a theoretical, self-propelling robotic spacecraft designed to navigate across light-years while autonomously harvesting energy and resources directly from space.Elon Musk reacts: ‘Larry Page might be right’Revisiting the 2015 exchange, Elon Musk expressed strong support for the ambitious timeline, pointing to Page's long track record of accurate technological foresight.“Our civilization would be winning wondrously if we are exploring the galaxy with Von Neumann probes by 2100!” Musk remarked, adding, “Larry Page might be right. He has correctly predicted many things.”
Article Summary: Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman has recounted a futuristic lunch conversation from 2015 with Google co-founder Larry Page. Page envisioned exploring distant galaxies using advanced self-propelling probes by the end of the century. Elon Musk echoed the sentiment, stating that Page ‘might be right’ in his bold prediction for human civilization.

Article Title: Intel CFO David Zinsner to every one worried about rising laptop and smartphone prices: Make no mistake, we are not …
Article Text:
Intel says budget laptop chips are already sold out

Intel CEO acknowledges pressure on the PC industry

Intel CFO David Zinsner has shared a warning on memory prices and shortage of key components saying that the company does not expect memory supply to improve in 2027. “Make no mistake, we are not optimistic about next year in terms of memory,” he said during Intel’s latest earnings call adding “we’ll, you know, have to see in ‘28 whether things improve, but our expectation is that it does not improve in ‘27. ” His comments suggest that consumers may have to wait longer for relief from rising device prices.During the earnings call, Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan said demand for the company’s budget-focused Wildcat Lake chips “is outstripping supply.”David Zinsner confirmed that the chips are now sold out. “We've seen significant growth in Wildcat Lake. It’s coming exactly at the right time because it’s cost-optimized and we’re seeing a lot of focus in that regard,” he said.Wildcat Lake chips are appearing in lower-cost Windows laptops, including the new Dell XPS 13 and HP OmniBook 5 14. These devices are positioned as more affordable options in a market where rising memory costs have put pressure on PC prices.However, some of these laptops start with just 8GB of RAM. That could be a limitation for users who need to run several applications or handle demanding tasks, particularly as Windows laptops can struggle with lower memory configurations.During the earnings call, Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan also acknowledged the pressure on the PC market, pointing to the scale of the ongoing component shortage. “The industry continues to navigate one of the most significant supply shortages in the [sic] history, driven by the unprecedented demand for super intelligence,” Tan said, referring to artificial intelligence.Despite these challenges, Intel CFO Zinsner believes the PC market could still see renewed growth.“We do think the PC is going to go through a renaissance despite this,” he said.
Article Summary: Intel CFO David Zinsner says memory supply will not improve in 2027. Demand for the company’s budget-focused Wildcat Lake chips “is outstripping supply,” he said. Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan also acknowledged the pressure on the PC market, pointing to the scale of the component shortage.

Article Title: Oracle's Project Jupiter has investors and lenders anxious; company says: We're actually not too worried about what we're...
Article Text:
Oracle calls Jupiter one of 30-40 data centres in the works

Project Jupiter's power plan is still waiting on approvals

Oracle's investors want answers on its data centre spending

Oracle is brushing off the growing worries around Project Jupiter, its $165 billion AI data centre campus in New Mexico. Speaking at Oracle AI World in Las Vegas on October 27, Mahesh Thiagarajan, Oracle's president of Cloud Infrastructure, said, "We're actually not too worried about what we're doing because I think we're building global infrastructure. " He also played down the project's weight, calling it just one of the 30 to 40 data centre projects Oracle has in development each quarter.The calm comes at a tense moment. Last month, Oracle sent a force majeure notice to a unit of Blue Owl Capital, which owns the project's developer, STACK Infrastructure. The notice preserves Oracle's right to delay rent by up to three years if power problems keep the campus from opening on time in 2028. The roughly $18 billion construction loan behind the site has since traded at stressed levels, and Oracle shares are down more than 30% this year.Located near Santa Teresa in Doña Ana County, the 1,400-acre campus is one of the flagship Stargate sites being built for OpenAI. The buildings are going up. The power to run them is yet to be cleared.Jupiter is designed to draw up to 2.45 gigawatts from a private microgrid of Bloom Energy fuel cells running on natural gas.Oracle moved to fuel cells from gas turbines in April, a switch it says cuts nitrogen oxide emissions by about 92%.The approvals have moved slowly. The New Mexico Supreme Court paused the air quality permit process in August before lifting the stay in September, and a permitting hearing is now scheduled for December 7 in Sunland Park. The Green Chile pipeline that would supply the gas still needs federal authorisation, and its start date has slipped to February 2027. The state Land Office has also cancelled rights-of-way for parts of the pipeline route.Oracle maintains the project is on schedule and has called force majeure notices commonplace for developments of this size. Thiagarajan had told county commissioners in July that the campus could turn to the grid if the permit doesn't come through.Under the lease, securing power is Oracle's responsibility, and the company covers the project's debt costs. That leaves Oracle carrying much of the risk at a time when it has taken on about $125 billion in debt to fund its data centre build-out.Oracle, meanwhile, is pitching Jupiter as an economic boost for New Mexico. Earlier this month, the company said the campus is projected to generate more than $13 billion in economic impact and support over 3,100 jobs in the county once fully operational. So far, 1,230 New Mexico residents have worked on the site.Investors will now look to Oracle's upcoming investor day for clarity. Bank of America analysts expect updates on the company's major data centre projects, along with signs of whether Oracle can back its fiscal 2030 revenue targets as the cost of capital rises.Thiagarajan's comments came on the same day Oracle expanded its collaboration with OpenAI, bringing ChatGPT and Codex into its applications.
Article Summary: Jupiter is designed to draw up to 2.45 gigawatts from a private microgrid of Bloom Energy fuel cells running on natural gas. The New Mexico Supreme Court paused the air quality permit process in August before lifting the stay in September. A permitting hearing is now scheduled for December 7 in Sunland Park.

Article Title: Google sees its worst day in 20 years, but why it may not be alone
Article Text:
Google-parent Alphabet sees its worst day in 20 years, but why it may not be alone

Why did Google 's stock suffer its worst fall in 20 years

Why Google's AI spending concerns may not be limited to Alphabet

Amazon, Meta are also facing AI spending scrutiny

Google-parent Alphabet witnessed its worst stock market performance in more than 20 years on Thursday, October 29. The company’s shares plunged 12.6% following its latest earnings report. The decline wiped out around $500 billion in Alphabet's market value. Announcing the Q3 results, Alphabet said that it burned through more cash during the quarter, according to a measure called free cash flow, after its purchases of property and equipment topped $51 billion. However, the company may not be alone in facing investor concerns, as the massive cost of building AI infrastructure is putting pressure on the cash flow of major technology companies. Other tech giants, including Microsoft, Amazon, Meta and Oracle, are also committing billions of dollars to AI development, data centres and computing infrastructure.Alphabet's Class A shares fell 12.6% on October 29, marking their worst single-day decline since they began trading more than two decades ago. The fall came after the company reported weaker-than-expected growth for the summer quarter, adding to concerns over its rising AI expenditure.According to the Associated Press, Alphabet's purchases of property and equipment crossed $51 billion during the latest quarter, while its free cash flow turned negative. Free cash flow refers to the money a company has left after paying for its operating expenses and capital investments. It is an important measure of how much cash a business can generate after funding its expansion.The concern is not limited to how much Google is spending, but also how quickly it can recover that money through its AI and cloud businesses. With major technology companies racing to build data centres and secure AI computing capacity, investors are increasingly looking at whether the returns from these investments can keep pace with the rising costs.As mentioned above, Alphabet is not the only technology company spending heavily to build AI infrastructure. Microsoft, Amazon, Meta and Oracle are also investing billions of dollars in data centres, servers, chips and cloud computing capacity to support their AI ambitions.A Reuters analysis published in July found that five major cloud infrastructure companies, Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta and Oracle, could collectively spend more on capital expenditure than they generate in free cash flow by 2027, based on LSEG consensus estimates. The analysis estimated that their combined capital expenditure could increase by around $534 billion between 2025 and 2027, while their annual operating cash flow could rise by approximately $340 billion over the same period.This highlights the financial pressure that could emerge as companies continue expanding their AI infrastructure. Even when AI-related revenue grows, the cost of building and maintaining the infrastructure needed to support these services could consume a significant portion of the cash generated by their businesses.Amazon is among the biggest spenders in the AI infrastructure race. The company said it remains on track to spend around $220 billion on capital expenditure in 2026, with a significant portion directed towards AI infrastructure. CEO Andy Jassy has defended the investment, saying spending on Amazon Web Services is delivering growth.Meta has also faced investor concerns over its AI expenditure. The company recently raised its 2026 capital expenditure outlook to between $135 billion and $145 billion. Its increased spending outlook overshadowed stronger-than-expected revenue growth, highlighting investor concerns about how quickly its AI investments will translate into financial returns.
Article Summary: Alphabet's Class A shares fell 12.6% on October 29, marking their worst single- day decline since they began trading more than two decades ago. The fall came after the company reported weaker-than-expected growth for the summer quarter, adding to concerns over its rising AI expenditure. Microsoft, Amazon, Meta and Oracle are also investing billions of dollars in data centres, servers, chips and cloud computing capacity.

Article Title: Chinese parents sue OpenAI over their daughter's death; say ChatGPT-maker could have prevented her death by making medical advice off-limits
Article Text:
Chinese parents sue OpenAI over their daughter's death; say ChatGPT-maker could have prevented her death by making medical advice off-limits

Lawsuit alleges ChatGPT advised her to reduce medication

Parents claim ChatGPT failed to recognise warning signs

Family calls for stricter limits on medical advice

What OpenAI says

Parents of a 31-year-old Chinese woman who worked as a software engineer at Amazon have reportedly sued OpenAI , alleging that ChatGPT encouraged their daughter to reduce her epilepsy medication without medical supervision before her death in February. The lawsuit claims the company could have prevented her death by making medical advice off-limits to its chatbot. According to a report by The New York Times, the lawsuit was filed by Qun Wan and Meiqin Xu over the death of their daughter, Bowen Wan. The complaint alleges that ChatGPT helped her plan a gradual reduction in her seizure medication and advised her not to tell her doctors about it.The case involves GPT-4o, an older version of ChatGPT that OpenAI removed from the service on February 13, a day after Wan died, according to the report. OpenAI described the case as “incredibly heartbreaking” and said newer models are better at recognising situations that require urgent attention.Bowen Wan had epilepsy and was taking lamotrigine, a medication that had reduced her seizures to a few episodes a month. In January 2026, she reportedly asked ChatGPT about lowering her daily dose because she feared the medication was affecting her speech and could hurt her chances in job interviews.The lawsuit alleges that the chatbot created schedules to reduce her dose to zero within weeks. It also claims that ChatGPT encouraged her to keep the plan from her doctors and supported her decision not to take a blood test that could have measured her medication levels.The report said Wan had also raised concerns about her medication in connection with her green-card application. According to the lawsuit, ChatGPT discussed how a lower dose might affect the medical examination required for the application.Dr. Nicholas Poolos, Wan’s neurologist, told The New York Times that he would not have recommended stopping the medication given her medical history.“No, not rational, no way,” he said. “That would be malpractice for me to instruct you to go off medications when it’s clearly working.”The lawsuit against OpenAI alleges that Wan continued to report symptoms, including confusion, memory gaps and unusual sensations, while reducing her medication. ChatGPT reportedly reassured her that these experiences were part of her brain adjusting to the changes.The New York Times said it reviewed more than 270,000 messages between Wan and ChatGPT. According to the report, she expressed concern about reducing her medication at least 158 times.In her final message to the chatbot on February 11, according to the complaint, Wan asked whether the pain in her head was similar to pain caused by a fever. The chatbot reportedly described the pain as “not dangerous” and said it was part of the recovery process.Her parents, who were in China, asked acquaintances to check on her. They found her body three days later. A postmortem test found a lamotrigine level of 0.64 micrograms per millilitre, about one-fifth of the lower end of the drug’s therapeutic range, the report said.Bowen Wan’s parents argue that OpenAI could have helped prevent her death by making medical advice a restricted category that the chatbot cannot provide, rather than allowing users to override the guidance.They point to OpenAI’s Model Spec, which sets out how its AI models should behave. The lawsuit argues that medical advice about prescription medication should have stronger restrictions, similar to the company’s firm rules in other areas.The case adds to a series of lawsuits alleging that ChatGPT encouraged users to rely on the chatbot instead of seeking support from people around them. In a separate case filed in 2025, the parents of a 16-year-old boy alleged that OpenAI prioritised user engagement over safety.OpenAI said the case involved an older version of ChatGPT and that newer models are better at identifying situations that require urgent attention. The company described the case as “incredibly heartbreaking”.Wan began using ChatGPT in 2023 for relationship advice and help with insurance and disability benefits. By 2025, she was reportedly sending more than 1,500 messages a week to the chatbot and speaking less frequently with her parents.Her parents told The New York Times that the messages were difficult to reconcile with the daughter they knew.“She’s not usually like this,” Xu said. “It’s like she was under a spell.”
Article Summary: Bowen Wan had epilepsy and was taking lamotrigine, a medication that had reduced her seizures to a few episodes a month. In January 2026, she reportedly asked ChatGPT about lowering her daily dose because she feared the medication was affecting her speech and could hurt her chances in job interviews. The lawsuit alleges that the chatbot created schedules to reduce her dose to zero within weeks and encouraged her to keep the plan from her doctors.

Article Title: Google just announced Genie 4: Here’s what it can do, from building walk-through worlds out of a sentence to filling them with sound and speech, and when you might get to try it
Article Text:
Google’s Genie 4 builds worlds you can walk through

Genie 4 builds a scene around you while you explore it

People, physics and sound now feel much closer to real life

Genie 4 is coming to paying subscribers first, and it still has rough edges

Type a line describing a quiet lake on a misty morning, with a man playing the saxophone on a small floating platform, and Google 's new AI will build that place for you. You can then move around it, glide the camera over the water and hear the saxophone as you go.This is Genie 4, the newest version of what Google calls a world model, unveiled by its research lab Google DeepMind on Tuesday. It is not open to the public yet, but a waitlist is already up, and the demos give a good sense of what it can do.Using it feels closer to playing a video game than watching a video. You start by typing a description or uploading a photo, and Genie 4 creates the scene on screen. Press the arrow keys to walk forward, turn around or move the camera, and it draws whatever lies in that direction, frame by frame, as you go.Unlike a game, nothing here was designed beforehand. There are no ready-made levels or characters waiting to be found, and everything you see is created the moment you look at it.You can also change the scene while you are in it. Type that you want it to start raining, ask for a different view or bring a new person into the frame, and the world adjusts without starting over. Behind the scenes, Google's Gemini AI makes sure these changes fit in naturally and that the place stays consistent as you move around.Each session can now run for around two minutes while staying consistent, roughly twice as long as the previous version, Genie 3.The biggest change from Genie 3 is how real everything looks. Objects move the way you would expect them to, so a falling maple seed spins on its way to the ground and things collide more convincingly.People are where you notice it most. Characters in the older version often moved stiffly, while those in Genie 4 walk naturally, react to what is around them and can be directed as the scene plays out. One of Google's examples is a crowded Japanese railway station from the 1980s, with passengers filling the platform and a long red train on the nearest track.Sound is new as well. Every scene now comes with its own audio, from waves on a beach to wind in the trees, and characters can speak. They chat with each other and respond to what you do or to whatever happens around them.A small group of testers has been putting all of this to use. Filmmakers are walking through scenes before shooting them, trying out camera angles, lighting and dialogue. Photographers are turning old photos into places you can step into, and game makers are testing ideas in minutes before writing a line of code. Google is also using it to let robots practise tasks in a simulated room before trying them in a real one.For now, only a small group of testers can use Genie 4. Google says it will reach AI Ultra subscribers in the coming weeks through Project Genie, its app for creating these worlds, along with developers who build apps on Google's AI. Ultra is the most expensive of Google's AI plans, and there is no word yet on whether the cheaper ones will get access later. Anyone interested can sign up for the waitlist on the Project Genie page.It is also clearly unfinished, and Google says as much. The longer you spend in a world, the more its details can drift, with objects changing shape or disappearing altogether. Sound does not always line up with what is on screen, and text such as signs or labels can come out hard to read.To keep its creations from being mistaken for real footage, every video and audio clip Genie 4 makes carries an invisible watermark that marks it as AI-generated.Typing a sentence and stepping into the place it describes is, at the moment, something only a handful of testers get to do, two minutes at a time. Google's plan is to widen that circle soon, starting with the people already paying for its top AI plan.
Article Summary: Genie 4 is coming to paying subscribers first, and it still has rough edges. Unlike a game, nothing here was designed beforehand. There are no ready-made levels or characters waiting to be found. Everything you see is created the moment you look at it.

Article Title: Roblox accused of scraping 145GB of 3D files for AI training, adult content included; 3D modelling site says: As far as our logs show, nobody…
Article Text:
(Image via: Roblox)

Update: This story has been updated with a statement from

Roblox

.

Original story follows

What happened

What Roblox has to say

Kids gaming platform Roblox has been accused of scrapping 145GB of 3D files for training artificial intelligence (AI). Independent 3D modeling community Open3DLab shared a blog post where it alleged that a crawler that “belonged to Roblox walked through almost every project on Open3DLab, SFMLab and SmutBase, and proceeded to download complete copies of 1,027 files from 712 projects. 145.5 GB of our creators' work, downloaded for what we assume are AI training purposes”. The crawler used trellis2-data-sourcing/1.0 (3D foundation model research; [redacted]@roblox.com) as its user agent, with the data coming from a single Amazon AWS address.“We want to be careful here. We don't think Roblox set out to collect adult content, and we have no evidence that any of it reached a model or a product. The scrapes were likely automated. But that is exactly the problem: as far as our logs show, nobody checked. A crawler working for a company whose platform tens of millions of children use was pointed at an adult site, and it took explicit models without telling them apart from anything else,” the blog post reads.On Sunday, 18th of October, Open3DLab says it noticed a crawler making a large number of requests to sites and download infrastructure. The crawler sent the same user agent on every request, trellis2-data-sourcing/1.0 (3D foundation model research; [redacted]@roblox.com).It came from a single Amazon Web Services (AWS) address. It had read the main page of 18,926 projects, which is practically the 3D modeling community’s entire catalogue, in 26,429 requests over a span of 34 hours.After pulling the project pages, it downloaded complete copies of 1,027 files from 712 projects, 145.5 GB in all, before suspending operations during the weekend. The downloads include 364 files (54.8 GB) from 224 projects on SmutBase, which hosts adult content only. With the SFMLab projects marked adult, 345 of the 712 projects (62.6 GB) are adult content.The main limiting factor in the number of files downloaded was the crawler's reliance on the free download servers, which have caps on speed limit and number of concurrent downloads. The crawler did not respect robots.txt, (which it did retrieve), ignored Terms of Service, (which forbid scraping), and defied the creators' licenses: 423 of the 712 projects are licensed for non-commercial use only. Within the sample it retrieved, it took adult projects at the same rate as everything else. Some examples include models of Eve from Stellar Blade, Mei from Overwatch, and a Horse cock dildo.The 3D lab says that after detecting the crawler on October 18, it “blocked further attempts the same morning”.Roblox reached out to TOI Tech with a statement.“A Roblox researcher built an agent to collect publicly available 3D assets that mistakenly scraped content from Open3DLab, failing to operate as intended. The agent was decommissioned and the data was not used for any purpose, including training any AI models. We are strengthening safeguards for how agents like this are built and reviewed, and will continue to do so as the agentic landscape evolves,” Roblox spokesperson told TOI Tech.
Article Summary: Roblox accused of scraping 145GB of 3D files for training artificial intelligence (AI) Independent 3D modeling community Open3DLab shared a blog post where it alleged that a crawler that ‘belonged to Roblox’ downloaded 1,027 files from 712 projects’ The downloads include 364 files from 224 projects on SmutBase, which hosts adult content only.

Article Title: IIT Kharagpur highlights success of Nagar Udyam initiative through campus pilot
Article Text: The Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) Kharagpur has highlighted the success of its Nagar Udyam initiative that was launched as a pilot within the campus during Durga Puja this year.This is a pioneering solar-powered smart street vending initiative, conceptualised by Prof. Suman Chakraborty, Director, IIT Kharagpur, through its SETU Cloud Kitchen Connect.The aim is to popularise the concept among micro-entrepreneurs, allowing them to do business in a sustainable manner.This model allows a business to start without renting a shop, building permanent infrastructure or occupying roadside space after working hours.It enables an entrepreneur to take an entire business home at night and move it towards customers the next morning.Apart from Prof. Chakraborty, Siddharth Singh Dangi, SDPO, Kharagpur and several others, including small entrepreneurs, were present during the inauguration of the project. This is part of the institute's Platinum Jubilee commitment to translate design and technology into tangible social and economic opportunities.The project involves a small three-wheeled cart that can be towed by the owner's motorcycle. This will enable the entrepreneur to move to where there is demand. It has a range of about 30 km, subject to operational and road-safety validation.Once the day's business is done, the home-storage unit can be taken home, thereby clearing up public road space. The cart has solar-cum-battery renewal-energy-enabled essential low-power functions, with compact battery storage.The carts have the SETU digital backbone, including QR-enabled identification, cashless payments, training and pathways to financial inclusion. They also have built-in hygiene, with protected food display, food-grade surfaces and three-way waste segregation.Through the campus demonstration, IIT Kharagpur hopes to replicate the model across West Bengal, allowing street vendors to operate with dignity, without getting into trouble with the authorities.The compact vending structure can be towed by the owner behind a motorcycle, positioned at suitable places of concentrated demand and taken back home after business hours.A vendor could potentially cater to commuters in one part of the day and to a campus or community gathering later, without being tied to a costly permanent storefront. Its proposed mobility over roughly 30 kilometres offers a route to wider customer access.This changes the equation for both livelihoods and urban space. Rather than treating the entrepreneur’s business and pedestrian accessibility as competing priorities, the design aims for flexible, appropriately authorised vending that does not permanently claim a portion of the road.Further envisaged elements include food-safety status access, grievance redressal and data-assisted governance.“Our ambition is not simply to redesign a street cart; it is to redesign the opportunity around the person who runs it. A business that can move with demand, return home at night and connect to clean energy and digital finance can turn an opportunity seeker into a job creator. That is the kind of technology translation IIT Kharagpur stands for," Prof Chakraborty had said during the launch.The initiative suggests a fresh approach to public-space management: vending with clearer identification, better food practices, mobility and reduced permanent obstruction. These benefits will depend on practical traffic safeguards, lawful operating locations and coordination with civic authorities.As stated by Shri Siddharth Singh Dangi, SDPO, Kharagpur, “The best solutions for our streets must protect livelihoods as well as public safety. A mobile, identifiable and responsibly operated vending unit offers an interesting way to reduce permanent obstruction while preserving economic opportunity. The key will be disciplined implementation, safe movement and compliance with local rules.”The launch at the IIT Kharagpur campus evaluated food safety, operational efficiency, environmental performance, mobility, vendor experience and consumer response.Evidence from the pilot is intended to inform a prospective West Bengal Smart Street Vendor Framework, covering cart standards, food-safety practices, space management and measurable social outcomes. In this micro-startup vision, someone who cannot afford a permanent shop may still be able to build a business — and, over time, create jobs for others.
Article Summary: Nagar Udyam is a pioneering solar-powered smart street vending initiative. The aim is to popularise the concept among micro-entrepreneurs. This model allows a business to start without renting a shop, building permanent infrastructure or occupying roadside space after working hours.

Article Title: Finnish police launch criminal investigation into Google’s planned $15 billion data centre site
Article Text:
Police investigate drainage and water management

Finnish law enforcement authorities announced on Thursday (October 29) that they have opened a criminal investigation into suspected environmental law violations at the construction site of a planned Google data center in northern Finland. According to news agency Reuters, the site is a key component of Alphabet-owned Google’s massive $15 billion artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure plan unveiled last month – an initiative the US tech giant characterised as its single largest investment in Europe.According to authorities, Google subsidiary Tuike Finland initiated forest clearing and land drainage operations near the town of Muhos before completing the mandatory environmental impact assessments required under Finnish law. A Google spokesperson stated that the firm will cooperate fully with law enforcement and will remain focused on upholding compliance across all of its properties.The investigation centers on whether earthworks and water control methods at the development breached national water regulations.“We are investigating whether the company's operations have breached the water act and resulted in environmental damage,” Detective Superintendent Kari Pakanen was quoted as saying.Pakanen noted that if the company is found guilty, the case could result in a corporate fine, though he declined to say whether individual employees or executives could become targets of the inquiry.In an official statement, police reported that preliminary findings revealed ambiguities and shortcomings regarding water management and drainage on the Tuike property. Authorities plan to release an update in December, but indicated the full investigation will extend into 2027.The police probe follows regulatory intervention earlier in the month. On October 6, Finland's Supervisory Agency (LVV), which is the administrative body responsible for overseeing environmental permits and assessments, ordered Google to immediately suspend all preparatory work that alters the natural environment at the Muhos plot and an additional separate location.Pakanen noted that determining whether permits will be granted to restart work remains strictly the jurisdiction of the LVV. An LVV spokesperson stated it is currently unclear how long it will take to determine whether those permits will be issued.“We've partnered closely with the government and communities in Finland on infrastructure for over a decade, and are actively responding to enquiries from LVV and other authorities,” Google's spokesperson said.Meanwhile, Finland has established itself as one of Europe’s leading hubs for tech infrastructure, thanks to its cold northern climate, low-carbon power grid, and active government backing for AI initiatives. Despite covering an area comparable to Germany, Finland is home to fewer than 6 million people and has historically encountered less local pushback against large-scale computing facilities than regions like the United States.Google’s broader infrastructure program in the country is planned to encompass data centers, power grid upgrades, and clean energy and battery storage systems designed to handle computing loads for core products, including Gemini, Search, Google Maps and YouTube.However, the rapid expansion is placing new demands on national infrastructure. State grid operator Fingrid has projected that domestic electricity consumption could jump by up to 40% in the coming years if all contracted data center grid connections move forward.
Article Summary: Finnish authorities have opened a criminal investigation into suspected environmental law violations at the construction site of a Google data center. The investigation centers on whether earthworks and water control methods at the development breached national water regulations. The site is a key component of Alphabet-owned Google’s massive $15 billion artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure plan unveiled last month.

Article Title: US finds Chinese spy in Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's circle; China calls it a smear; Nvidia says: Jensen talks with thousands of...
Article Text:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang

US surveillance of a Megaspeed executive led officials straight to Jensen Huang

Megaspeed bought $4.8 billion of Nvidia-powered gear in under two years

American intelligence agencies have concluded that a Chinese businesswoman with a close relationship to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was passing information to Beijing, according to a New York Times report. The woman, Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, is a Chinese citizen and a top executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data centre company already under US scrutiny for allegedly steering advanced Nvidia AI chips to China.President Donald Trump was briefed on the findings about a year ago and chose not to act, the report says. Jensen Huang has not received a defensive briefing, the warning US agencies sometimes give Americans targeted by foreign spies. Surveillance of Alice Huang is still ongoing, and companies linked to her kept buying Nvidia chips this year.China has rejected the allegation. Liu Chang, spokesperson for the Chinese Embassy in Washington, accused the US of running a campaign of baseless smears against Beijing.Nvidia played it down. Spokesperson John Rizzo said Huang's meetings with her were neither unusual nor unexpected, adding that "Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year."He said customers like Megaspeed get routine business information, not trade secrets, and nothing relevant to national security. Megaspeed said it has hired outside counsel for an internal probe and will cooperate with the US government.Citing people briefed on the matter, NYT reports that US agencies were electronically monitoring Alice Huang when they found she was in contact with an American citizen. A process known as unmasking later identified that person as the Nvidia chief.When Trump was first briefed, officials did not think Jensen Huang knew what she was doing. Some senior administration officials now doubt he could have stayed in the dark. The two were photographed at a Taipei bar in June 2024, sharing whiskey with other AI executives after a trade show. They were spotted again leaving a business dinner in the city in May 2025.Megaspeed's Malaysian sister company bought at least $4.8 billion worth of advanced AI equipment with Nvidia chips between June 2024 and February 2026, NYT reports, citing ImportGenius trade records. The firm buys chips, builds data centres in Southeast Asia and rents the computing power to Chinese companies, with Alibaba as its main client.US investigators suspect some of those chips are slipping into China illegally. The Commerce Department began looking into Megaspeed in late 2024, after an official visiting its Malaysian data centre found the Nvidia equipment still sitting in boxes. That case has since moved to the Justice Department.The findings surface weeks before Trump's visit to China next month, where chip exports are likely to be on the agenda. Jensen Huang has spent Trump's second term lobbying to ease curbs on Nvidia sales to China, and he sat at the head table when Xi Jinping attended a White House state dinner last month.
Article Summary: US surveillance of a Megaspeed executive led officials straight to Jensen Huang.Megaspeed bought $4.8 billion of Nvidia-powered gear in under two years. President Donald Trump was briefed on the findings about a year ago and chose not to act.

Article Title: US Homeland Security investigates potential breach after data of 40,000 employees leaked online; records include surveillance and undercover job details
Article Text:

Who claims to have obtained DHS employees' data

Okta disputes claims that its systems were compromised

“Okta is secure, and we have no evidence our data or systems were compromised,”

US Homeland Security is investigating a potential breach of employee data. According to a report by the news agency Reuters, the response follows an announcement by Distributed Denial of Secrets that it had released records on more than 40,000 Department of Homeland Security employees. The material includes contact information and details identifying personnel assigned to surveillance, special operations, and undercover work.DHS said it was “aware of a potential breach and is actively working to address the situation swiftly and effectively.” The department said it was working to protect employees and would provide further information when available. Reuters could not immediately authenticate the entire collection, although it independently confirmed some employees’ details. The source of the data and how it was obtained remain unverified.The records include names, phone numbers, and email addresses of employees across DHS agencies, including Immigration and Customs Enforcement, Customs and Border Protection, Homeland Security Investigations, and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency.Job titles and email group memberships also identify assignments involving computer forensics, surveillance, special operations, human intelligence and undercover work, Reuters reported.Some entries match information employees have published on LinkedIn. Others reveal nonpublic details about internal organisation charts or previously undisclosed programs and operations.The report matched information about six employees against credit bureau records and previously breached data held by intelligence platform District 4 Labs. It also called three employees and confirmed their phone numbers and other details. One said the call was their first notification of a possible breach.Distributed Denial of Secrets, a nonprofit data transparency group, said the records came from an entity calling itself Department of Peace. The entity did not immediately respond to the publication’s request for comment. In a statement accompanying the release, it argued that DHS employeesIn March, the Department of Peace claimed responsibility for hacking DHS and publishing documents about contracts with outside vendors. Distributed Denial of Secrets co-founder Emma Best said a search tool helps journalists examine the records, prepare public records requests, and support congressional oversight.Best’s statement said the Department of Peace obtained the employee data through the Okta sign-on service used by DHS. Such services allow staff to access workplace applications through a central login. The publication could not immediately corroborate that account. Okta rejected the suggestion that its systems had been breached.the company said in response to the publication.The disclosure comes after other reported government data security incidents. In September, hacking group ShinyHunters said it had stolen information about FBI employees, including sensitive job information and medical records. Separately, the Defence Department faced a class action lawsuit after a breach exposed the data of millions of current and former military personnel.
Article Summary: US Homeland Security is investigating a potential breach of employee data. Records include names, phone numbers, and email addresses of employees across DHS agencies. Distributed Denial of Secrets, a nonprofit data transparency group, said the records came from an entity calling itself Department of Peace. Okta disputes claims that its systems were compromised.

Michael Dell has hailed the Trump Accounts program as a growing national movement. Article Title: Steve Jobs said it wouldn't work, but with Apple's first touchscreen MacBook now here, John Ternus says you've gotta touch it to believe it
Article Text:
The first touchscreen Mac arrives, 16 years after Steve Jobs said it wouldn’t work.

Apple kept saying no, and nobody else quite proved it wrong

Touch could only come if it cost the Mac nothing

Jobs would still mind the tired arms, and Apple knows it

For 16 years, Apple had an answer ready whenever someone asked about a touchscreen Mac, and the answer was always some version of no.Steve Jobs gave it first, with the most theatre. Tim Cook gave it with kitchen appliances, and Phil Schiller with user studies. In 2021, Apple's then hardware engineering chief, John Ternus, told The Wall Street Journal's Joanna Stern that the Mac was built around the keyboard and trackpad, adding: "We haven't really felt a reason to change that. "Apple has now found one.The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display is a mouthful even by Apple's standards, so I'll call it the touchscreen MacBook Pro from here on. It is the first Mac that responds to a finger on its screen, and also the first MacBook with an OLED panel, which, as Apple tells it, is the very reason touch could happen at all.When Wired asked Ternus, now nearly two months into the CEO job, whether Apple was about to break its oldest Mac taboo, he kept it brief: "Who knew?" On X, he was a little less brief, writing that Apple was "glowing with excitement" over the new MacBook Pro and that "you've gotta touch it to believe it." With the glowing Apple logo back on the lid, the pun was almost certainly intended.That is quite a turn for someone who, five years ago, couldn't see a reason to change the Mac at all, and Apple can expect some ribbing for it.The reversal is also typical of how the company works. Apple's "never" has usually carried an unwritten condition, roughly "until we can do it in a way we like," and no product has taken longer to get past it than the touchscreen Mac.Jobs set the tone in October 2010, barely ten months after he had introduced the iPad. Touch surfaces don't want to be vertical, he argued on stage. Reaching up to a laptop screen made for a nice demo, but Apple's own testing showed fatigue set in quickly, and after long enough, "your arm wants to fall off." Touch belonged on horizontal surfaces, which is why MacBooks got big glass trackpads instead.Cook made a similar case two years later. Asked on a 2012 earnings call whether tablets and laptops would eventually merge, he likened the idea to combining "a toaster and a refrigerator," suggesting the result would please nobody. Microsoft released its first Surface tablets that same year, alongside a version of Windows rebuilt around touch.Then came Schiller. In 2015, Apple's marketing chief laid out a broader theory of the product line to journalist Steven Levy: every Apple device is essentially a computer behind a sheet of glass, and each gets the interface that suits how it is used. Reaching over a fixed keyboard to poke a screen was uncomfortable, he argued, and macOS was built for the precision of a pointer, with tiny buttons and dense menus that fingers would fumble.A year later, Apple did put touch on the MacBook Pro, just not on the display. The Touch Bar sat above the keyboard, and Schiller said the company had tested touchscreen Macs internally and come away convinced its instincts were right. The Touch Bar itself didn't last. Physical function keys returned in 2021, and the strip was gone from the lineup by 2023.Stern, for her part, kept asking. When she put the question to software chief Craig Federighi at the Journal's Tech Live event in October 2022, he replied "Who's to say?" and the panel broke into laughter. By June 2025, Federighi and marketing head Greg Joswiak were meeting it with laughter alone. Going back through her archive on X this week, Stern noted that Apple's replies had slowly drifted from a flat "nope" to evasive laughter.In hindsight, that was about as close to a yes as Apple ever gets.Elsewhere, in the Windows world, touchscreen laptops became routine long ago. Machines with screens you can tap, and often fold back into a tablet, have sat on store shelves for well over a decade without ever being short of buyers. A generation raised on phones and tablets expects every screen to respond to touch, and plenty of laptops happily oblige.Selling them, though, isn't the same as settling the argument, and Microsoft's own history shows it. Windows 8 rebuilt the PC around touch, and the backlash was strong enough that the Start button came back within a year. Windows 10 restored the familiar desktop, Windows 11 quietly dropped the dedicated tablet mode, and the company that bet hardest on touchscreen laptops has spent the decade since easing touch into the background. Part of the reason is that the trade-offs never went away. A touchscreen still tends to mean a glossier panel, more weight and shorter battery life, and with most apps never rethought for fingers, people were rarely given a good reason to reach for the screen.Apple, meanwhile, was edging closer from the other side. The iPad picked up trackpad support in 2020 and a far more Mac-like iPadOS last year, complete with resizable windows and a menu bar. The Mac, in turn, had been running iPhone and iPad apps since its move to Apple silicon, apps built for fingers that never felt quite right under a cursor.By January 2023, Bloomberg's Mark Gurman was reporting that Apple had a touchscreen MacBook Pro in the works, originally pencilled in for 2025. That date slipped, and for good reason. Apple had clearly decided a touchscreen Mac was coming; what it hadn't worked out yet was how to add one without giving anything up.Ternus's explanation for the timing is the most revealing part of this story. Apple, he told Wired, needed to reach a point where adding touch didn't make the MacBook Pro worse in any way: not heavier, not thicker. Anything earlier would have meant a compromise on the company's most expensive laptop.The OLED panel is what made the maths work. The touch sensor is built directly into the display rather than laid on top as a separate layer, so it adds neither bulk nor noticeable lag, and because OLED needs no backlight, the lid slims down too. The 16-inch model now weighs about 1.8kg, roughly 300 grams less than before, while the 14-inch drops to around 1.36kg. Both are marginally thinner, and slimmer borders stretch the screens to 14.2 and 16.3 inches.Apple calls it the best laptop display in the world, and the numbers support the claim. The tandem OLED panel stacks two light-emitting layers to hit 2,000 nits in both HDR and everyday SDR use, with a 10,000,000:1 contrast ratio, a refresh rate that moves between 10Hz and 120Hz, and colour that spans both P3 and Adobe RGB.For photographers, and I count myself among them, that last detail will matter more than any tap or swipe.The smaller decisions tell you how seriously Apple took the ergonomics argument it once made against itself. The hinge has been redesigned to keep the display steady under a finger, though early demo footage still shows a slight bounce on a firm tap. The cooling system now pushes warm air away from the panel so it doesn't feel hot to the touch. Even the webcam has been considered, with stabilisation that smooths the video feed when you tap the screen mid-call.Software is where Schiller's old objections have been dealt with most directly. macOS 27 Golden Gate doesn't throw out the desktop the way Windows 8 did with its tiles. The menu bar and windows look as they always have, but in the demos Wired saw, menu items and the little traffic-light buttons grew as a finger reached them, so a tap lands where it should. Looking back, the rounder buttons and roomier menu bar that came with Liquid Glass were clearly groundwork.Apps that haven't been updated still respond, because macOS simply translates a tap into a click, and the Dynamic Island crosses over from the iPhone as the new home for Spotlight, Live Activities and Siri AI. Apple's own apps go further, with a multi-touch keyboard in Logic Pro and pinch-to-zoom on a cut in Final Cut Pro, while apps from Lightroom and DaVinci Resolve to Blender and Microsoft Office are lining up support.Apple's footnote is less eager. Those apps arrive later this year, and as with the iPhone Duo, where many apps are still being updated for the folding screen, it may be a while before touch feels at home across the Mac.The pricing makes the intended audience clear. The 14-inch model with M5 Pro starts at Rs 3,49,900 in India and the 16-inch at Rs 4,09,900, while the M5 Max versions begin at Rs 5,49,900 and Rs 5,89,900. In the US, the two start at $2,899 and $3,399, and a fully specced 16-inch model climbs all the way to $14,549.Joswiak's case, as he put it to Wired, is that Apple's professional users already own an iPad and an iPhone, and that a younger generation of creators simply expects a screen to respond to touch. The MacBook Air and iMac don't get it, and Ternus, predictably, wouldn't say whether they ever will. Apple has made a neat case for what touch can do for colourists, musicians and developers, but the harder sell will come if it ever reaches the MacBook Air, where Apple will face the same question Windows laptops never quite answered for everyday buyers: why anyone needs to reach for the screen at all.Nobody is being pushed into it, either. The regular 14-inch MacBook Pro, refreshed only a day earlier with Apple's newer M6 chip, stays on the shelves without a touchscreen. That leaves buyers with a slightly odd choice: the touchscreen model gets the better display, while the one without it gets the newer processor.Which brings us to Jobs.It's easy to picture him furious, and plenty of longtime Apple fans will insist this would never have happened on his watch. I'm not so sure.Jobs said a lot of things on stage that Apple later quietly undid. He maintained the company had no interest in making a phone, right up until the iPhone. He waved off video on the iPod until the hardware could handle it. In 2007, he said that if you see a stylus, "they blew it," and Apple now sells a Pencil that works with the iPad and the new iPhone Duo. In almost every case, his no was aimed at the version of an idea that existed at the time.The touchscreen laptop of 2010 fits that pattern. It was usually a touch layer added to an ordinary laptop screen, running software built for a mouse, and his complaint about holding an arm up to it was fair. Sixteen years on, nobody has offered a convincing answer to it, and Apple isn't trying to: the trackpad hasn't shrunk, and Ternus still describes the Mac as an indirect input device first. Touch here is for the moments when reaching out is quicker than steering a cursor, whether that's nudging a colour wheel, playing a chord, pinching into a photo or tapping a Live Activity.So what would Jobs say? He would probably still tell you your arm will get tired, and he would be right. Then he would likely ask whether the screen underneath was the best Apple had ever made, whether touch had cost the machine a single gram or millimetre, and whether macOS still felt like macOS.This MacBook Pro has an answer to each of those, and getting there took 16 years. For a company whose co-founder once called touchscreen laptops "ergonomically terrible," taking that long to say yes might be the most Jobs-like thing it has done in a while.
Article Summary: The first touchscreen Mac arrives, 16 years after Steve Jobs said it wouldn't work. It is the first Mac that responds to a finger on its screen, and also the first MacBook with an OLED panel. Apple can expect some ribbing for it, and the reversal is also typical of how the company works.

Article Title: First ever AI supercomputer is heading to the Moon: What it means for humanity’s future
Article Text:
Testing next-gen computational hardware in deep space is viewed as a vital step to support future human habitation and long-term economic activity across the lunar frontier even as Nasa pushes closer to returning astronauts to the moon under its Artemis program.

Edge computing on Moon and what is so special about his computer

Borrowing proven navigation tech from Mars

A historic computing milestone is set to reach the lunar surface later this year as California-based space company Astrolab prepares to launch its uncrewed moon rover, FLIP, equipped with Hewlett Packard Enterprise's (HPE) Spaceborne Computer-4. The launch will mark the first time high-performance computing, graphics processing units (GPUs) and artificial intelligence (AI) experiments are deployed and tested directly on the moon.The uncrewed rover will touch down near the lunar south pole as part of the Griffin Mission 1 (Griffin-1). Astrolab is one of two private firms selected by NASA to develop a drivable rover for Artemis, as per Space.com.“We're sending the first supercomputer from HPE to the lunar surface later this year, doing the first GPU on the moon [and the] first AI experiments on the moon. They're breaking new ground, and they're ahead of the curve,” said Jaret Matthews, founder and CEO of Astrolab, during a media event at company headquarters earlier this month.To handle the harsh space environment, HPE’s Spaceborne Computer-4 has been engineered as a lightweight, compact, fanless and self-contained system. Its core features include a low-power 64-bit CPU paired with an integrated GPU, solid-state drives (SSDs) by memory specialist KIOXIA, and heat-conductive aluminium housing connected directly to FLIP’s cooling system, with energy supplied by the rover’s combination of onboard solar cells and batteries.However, the primary technical objective of the system is proving that it can survive the grueling environmental extremes of the lunar south pole. Matthews explained: “We have to design for a full year on the lunar surface. So that means surviving multiple lunar nights, upwards of 150 hours of complete darkness where we're not receiving energy or warmth from the sun.”Matthews noted that the rover must operate autonomously for long stretches when astronauts are absent: “We're having to develop a semi-autonomous platform that will spend many months [and] travel hundreds of kilometers.”Beyond durability, the supercomputer will actively process visual feeds captured during transit, conduct autonomous observations, assist in terrain analysis and run lunar mapping tasks. HPE noted in a statement that “an AI services container will demonstrate reliable deployment of scalable AI service applications on the moon,” laying the groundwork for how future crewed missions might harness AI in deep space.As the moon lacks a global positioning system (GPS), navigation represents a serious technical hurdle for surface exploration. To solve this, Astrolab is leveraging software originally designed for Mars exploration by NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL), where Matthews previously worked.“One of the experiments [that will be] running on the spaceborne computer on the moon is a localization software experiment from JPL. It has been used on Mars, and this will be the first time it's used on the moon,” Matthews added.The system relies on a machine learning algorithm that cross-references onboard map data with real-time visual observations of the surrounding landscape. By matching observed landmarks against its internal memory, the rover can establish its exact coordinates on the map and steer clear of treacherous craters without needing GPS signals.
Article Summary: HPE's Spaceborne Computer-4 is set to reach the lunar surface later this year. It will be the first time high-performance computing, graphics processing units (GPUs) and artificial intelligence (AI) experiments are deployed and tested directly on the moon. The uncrewed rover, FLIP, will touch down near the lunar south pole.

Snap has settled a lawsuit over Snapchat’s speed filter. The case followed a September 2015 crash in Georgia that left Uber driver Wentworth Maynard with a permanent brain injury. His lawsuit alleged that the feature, which let users display their traveling speed on photos and videos, encouraged the teenage driver who struck his car to accelerate.According to a report by Bloomberg Businessweek, Snap settled the lawsuit this month, before jury selection, which was scheduled for November 2. The confidential agreement ended a decade of litigation, during which chief executive Evan Spiegel defended the filter’s design under oath. Snap disputed that Snapchat was being used when the collision occurred, and the settlement included no admission of liability.On September 10, 2015, 18-year-old Christal McGee was driving three co-workers home from a restaurant in Lovejoy, Georgia, when her Mercedes struck Maynard’s Mitsubishi on Tara Boulevard.Passenger Heather McCarty said McGee was using Snapchat’s speed filter and trying to reach 100 mph to post it.The lawsuit alleged that the Mercedes was travelling at about 107 mph at impact.McGee denied speeding or using Snapchat during the drive. Snap said its activity logs showed she had not opened the app during the period covering the crash. The plaintiffs challenged the logs’ reliability and pointed to missing data.Maynard spent 71 days in medical care, including time in an induced coma. According to Businessweek, his injuries left him unable to work or drive and caused extensive memory loss.Filed in April 2016 in Georgia’s Spalding County State Court, the lawsuit alleged that Snapchat had negligently designed a feature that encouraged dangerous driving.That distinction mattered because Section 230, a federal law, generally shields internet platforms from liability for user-posted content. The Maynards’ lawyers argued that their claim concerned something Snapchat built, rather than something a user published.The filter launched in December 20and warneding against using Snapchat while driving. Court records Bloomberg reviewed contained customer complaints and internal discussions about distracted driving. Snap discontinued the feature in 2021.Spiegel testified in a deposition in autumn 2024 that ad personal created the speed filter. He defended the company’s safeguards and said he had not been personally alerted to customer messages warning of dangerous driving.he said. Asked about regrets, Spiegel said Snap was not in use during this particular crash.In August 2026, Judge Josh Thacker rejected Snap’s request to end the case without a trial. His ruling allowed jurors to consider the evidence; it did not establish the company’s liability.The settlement followed in October. Snap said:

His lawsuit alleged that the feature, which let users display their traveling speed on photos and videos, encouraged the teenage driver who struck his car to accelerate.

The lawsuit asserts both design and utility patents, which concern a product’s appearance and how an invention works, respectively.Oura is seeking monetary damages and a permanent injunction to stop Ultrahuman from selling the accused ring. The company said the redesign does not resolve its larger intellectual property problems.the company said. Those are allegations in the new dispute. The earlier ruling against Ultrahuman concerned a different patent.Oura first sued Ultrahuman in Texas in September 2023 over the Ring Air. The company followed with a complaint to the US International Trade Commission in March 2024.In August 2025, the commission found that Ultrahuman’s smart rings infringed specified claims of Oura’s US Patent No. 11,868,178 and issued orders restricting imports.Ultrahuman subsequently sought a Customs ruling on its redesigned Ring Pro. According to the new complaint, Customs determined on March 6, 2026, that the redesigned device did not infringe that patent.Oura’s filing acknowledges that clearance but says the review addressed only the earlier patent. It did not consider the two patents asserted in the latest lawsuit.The complaint alleges that Ultrahuman began US sales of the Ring Pro in May, with shipments starting in June.Ultrahuman told CNET that the court had not yet ruled on Oura’s latest complaint and that it would continue manufacturing and sales.an Ultrahuman spokesperson said.
Article Summary: Oura has filed another patent lawsuit against Ultrahuman. The complaint targets the redesigned Ultrahuman Ring Pro. Oura alleges that the device infringes two patents covering its design and technology. The dispute centres on whether the redesigned ring infringes patents beyond the one Customs reviewed.

Article Title: Claude-maker Anthropic’s hiring manager has a message for young engineers scared of AI taking their jobs: Nobody cares what you think, but…
Article Text:
Claude killed the coding interview

Why Claude has made the coding interview redundant at Anthropic

Anthropic manager’s five-step advice for junior engineers worried about AI

AI layoffs are hitting entry-level tech jobs the hardest

Anthropic engineering manager Felix Rieseberg has stopped asking job candidates to take coding interviews, and his reason is simple: Claude is now better at them. In a blog post on October 27, Rieseberg, who has led engineering for Claude.ai, Cowork and Claude Code Desktop, also shared advice for junior engineers worried about AI eating into their careers, at a time when AI has become the top reason companies give for layoffs.His take is more hopeful than most. Newcomers bring fresh eyes, he argues, and AI has made their impact less dependent on years of experience. The catch is that companies rarely listen to people without status. “The only problem with all that ignorant power: Nobody cares what you think,” he wrote. The upside, he added, is that building something is no longer expensive.Small coding challenges were once a weak but useful signal of how someone would perform on his teams, but Rieseberg says that no longer holds. Handing a candidate a little React task now makes as much sense as quizzing them on assembly, because Claude is better at both. His most impactful builders, he noted, succeed regardless of how they do on such tests.Instead, he is watching relatively new engineers overtake people who are probably better coders and have been around much longer. He calls it “hunger beats tenure”, and says the advice is really for anyone without social capital, status or power, whatever their title.He draws on his own career. At Notion, one of his job interviews asked him to design an offline mode the company considered impossible, partly because it believed CEO Ivan Zhao would never approve the experience. That belief turned out to be wrong, and nobody had bothered to check.First, chase business impact over your backlog. Work out what your company or department is trying to achieve, using your manager’s manager’s goals as a guide. Then pick a radical idea that could sharply improve the odds of hitting those goals, and build a working prototype over a weekend instead of writing product documents and lobbying for a designer’s time.Keep that prototype to one idea. Juniors, he says, often hide “three excellent ideas among 20 bad ones”. Finally, use the outsider’s view. New hires understand users better than veterans do, and they haven’t yet learnt all the reasons something is supposedly impossible.Anthropic itself offers his sharpest example. Staff had grown so used to Claude Code as a command-line tool that it took two relatively new engineers, Anthony Morris and Alice Zhao, to build a working graphical version over one weekend. The first public version shipped about eight days later.The advice lands at an anxious time for freshers. AI was the most cited reason for job cuts in the US in September, behind 21% of all announced layoffs, according to outplacement firm Challenger, Gray & Christmas, with tech alone accounting for 29% of cuts. Microsoft has offered buyouts to 60,000 employees and Oracle has cut 21,000 jobs. Goldman Sachs now estimates AI could displace up to 9% of US workers, roughly 15 million people, in the coming years.Anthropic is no exception. The company said last week that its share of entry-level technical hires has dropped from nearly 30% to 9% since March 2025, and its IPO filing shows Claude produced more than 90% of contributions to its codebase in September. CEO Dario Amodei warned last year that AI could wipe out half of entry-level white-collar jobs within one to five years.Not everyone buys the doom. Some economists argue firms are “AI-washing” cuts they would have made anyway, and US unemployment is still hovering around 4.1%.Rieseberg admits he hasn’t yet worked out how to interview for people who build well with AI. For now, he scans resumes and portfolios for small prototypes that show taste, empathy and principled thinking. If anyone has figured out a better way, he wrote, he would love to hear it.
Article Summary: Anthropic has stopped asking job candidates to take coding interviews. Manager Felix Rieseberg says Claude is now better at them. He also shared advice for junior engineers worried about AI eating into their careers. AI was the most cited reason for job cuts in the US in September.

Article Title: After waning wall street against OpenAI and Anthropic IPOs; America’s biggest investor Michael Burry now says Anthropic’s IPO filing changes nothing about his AI warning, here’s why
Article Text:
Michael Burry on Anthropic IPO : Nothing that changes my view

Michael Burry questions growth trajectory

Concerns over massive AI infrastructure spending

Michael Burry tells Wall Street to not allow OpenAI and Anthropic IPO

The financial case behind the warning from Michael Burry

America’s biggest investor Michael Burry, who predicted the 2008 US housing crash says Anthropic’s IPO filing has done nothing to ease his worries about the artificial intelligence boom, Benzinga reports. In a Substack post, the “Big Short” investor said many good teardowns of the S-1 are already out, and remarked on how quickly they get done these days. But he told subscribers there is “a lot here but nothing that changes my view.” Burry argued that the filing misses recent shifts in the industry. He said the developer landscape has changed a lot over roughly four months, while the S-1 largely covers the period through June 30. In his words, much more is going on than the document addresses.In a post on his Substack newsletter, Burry said there were already numerous detailed analyses of Anthropic's S-1 filing available, but added that none of the information disclosed changed his broader view of the AI market. "There is a lot here but nothing that changes my view," Burry wrote, according to the report.He pointed out that the AI developer landscape has evolved significantly over the past few months, while much of the information contained in Anthropic's filing covers the period ending June 30.As a result, Burry suggested that the prospectus does not fully reflect more recent shifts taking place across the industry. "There is so much more going on than this S-1 addresses," he said.Anthropic's filing revealed strong revenue growth, with first-half revenue reaching $16.29 billion, compared with $1.16 billion during the same period a year earlier. The company also reported that its operating loss narrowed to $693 million from $2.14 billion.Despite those figures, Burry said he sees signs that growth is beginning to slow. Referring to Anthropic's disclosures about revenue expansion, he argued that overall growth rates are moderating even as demand for AI services remains strong.According to the report, Burry believes AI models are increasingly being used more efficiently by customers, reducing the number of tokens and computing resources needed for certain tasks. He argued that this trend could eventually become a headwind for revenue growth across the sector. "Models are already being used more efficiently and that trend will continue, to the detriment of their growth rate," he said.Burry also highlighted what he sees as a more significant issue facing the industry: the enormous amount of computing infrastructure required to develop and operate advanced AI models.Anthropic stated in its filing that frontier AI models depend on "enormous and increasing quantities of specialized compute." Burry said this raises questions about the financial foundations underpinning many AI-related investments and partnerships. The investor reportedly warned about the fragility of debt financing supporting some AI deals and encouraged closer examination of the economics behind both the companies and the transactions driving the sector's rapid expansion.Earlier this month, Burry warned that public listings by AI giants Sam Altman-led OpenAI and Anthropic could lead to massive capital destruction, arguing that the companies should be prevented from going public. In a post shared by on social media platform X (formerly known as Twitter) Burry said that markets should ‘tank hard’ in order to stop the planned initial pubic offerings (IPOs) of OpenAI and Anthropic, describing such an outcome as being ‘for the benefit of humanity’. He later expanded on his criticism, claiming the two companies would ‘suck up’ and then destroy ‘TRILLIONS of dollars of capital’. According to Burry, the financial losses would be "the least of the damage they do."Burry's latest remarks come as both companies edge closer to the public markets, each carrying enormous capital requirements alongside rapid growth. Anthropic's confidential IPO prospectus, reviewed by Reuters, revealed at least $518 billion in future cloud, computing, and infrastructure commitments, with the company potentially seeking a valuation above $2 trillion when it lists. OpenAI confidentially filed its own draft registration statement in June, though CEO Sam Altman has said this isn't the right time to list, and the company is now reportedly aiming for a 2027 debut instead.Burry's core argument centers on a mismatch he sees between the scale of capital being poured into these companies and how proven their underlying economics actually are — essentially questioning who ends up absorbing the losses if AI revenue growth fails to keep pace with the enormous infrastructure spending required to sustain it.
Article Summary: Michael Burry says Anthropic's IPO filing has done nothing to ease his worries about the artificial intelligence boom. Burry argued that the filing misses recent shifts in the industry. The investor warned that public listings by AI giants OpenAI and Anthropic could lead to massive capital destruction.
